findings.heading: Tables
findings.proposition: The English warns that flextable functions MAY PRODUCE tables that are shortened or cut off, a reason to prefer knitr::kable(). The Japanese instead states that using flextable functions you CAN CREATE summary tables and tables with a portion cut off, presenting the same behaviour as a capability rather than a drawback.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reads the sentence as an endorsement of flextable and may use it for dashboard panels, then gets silently truncated tables in the panel with no warning that this was the documented failure mode.

findings.heading: Section attributes
findings.proposition: The English names the section attribute `{data-navbar=}` for nesting a page inside a navigation-bar drop-down menu; the Japanese names `{data-navmenu=}` for the same purpose.
findings.reader_consequence: The two editions teach different attribute names for the same feature. A reader comparing the editions, or an editor syncing them, cannot tell which is authoritative. (The Japanese name is the one flexdashboard actually accepts, and it matches the English text at line 197, so the English bullet is the wrong one.)

findings.heading: Interactive plots
findings.proposition: The Japanese states the interactive functionality can be displayed even without an internet connection. The English only states it still works if the dashboard is emailed as a static file (not online on a server), and makes no claim about internet connectivity.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes an offline-rendering guarantee from the handbook that the English never gives, and may ship a dashboard to offline users without testing it, when the guarantee actually depends on whether the widget's JavaScript is self-contained.

findings.heading: HTML widgets
findings.proposition: The Japanese states that the htmlwidgets.org web page contains many samples of HTML widgets. The English only defines what HTML widgets are and where they can be embedded; it makes no claim about the content of the linked page.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader follows the link expecting a sample gallery. This is extra propositional content the English author did not write, so it is not maintained when the linked site changes.

findings.heading: Tables
findings.proposition: The English lists paging as a DT::datatable() capability: the user can click through the 'pages' of the data frame. The Japanese moves the word 'page' to mean the dashboard page ('within a page, the user can filter, sort and operate') and states no paging capability.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn that the DT table paginates the data frame, so the `pageLength = 5` setting described two paragraphs later has no stated purpose and may be read as a hard limit of 5 displayed records.

findings.heading: YAML
findings.proposition: The Japanese states that a value must be quoted if it contains a colon OR OTHER SYMBOLS SUCH AS BRACKETS. The English states only the colon case.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader learns a broader quoting rule than the handbook establishes and than YAML requires, and may quote values unnecessarily or, worse, generalise the rule wrongly to other punctuation.

findings.heading: Code chunks
findings.proposition: The English gives three ways to create a new code chunk: typing it out yourself, the keyboard shortcut, and the green insert icon. The Japanese gives only the keyboard shortcut and the green icon.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is not told that the chunk delimiters can simply be typed by hand, so a reader without the RStudio toolbar (for example editing the .Rmd in a plain text editor) is left with no offered method.

findings.heading: Layout
findings.proposition: The English gives the heading markers as '#, ##, or ###'. The Japanese gives them as '#、##、##', repeating the second-level marker and never naming the third-level marker.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader taking the layout summary at face value does not learn from it that charts are added with a third-level (###) heading, and may write a second '##' where a '###' is required, producing an extra row or column instead of a chart panel.

findings.heading: Tabs
findings.proposition: The English says the same tabbing works with rows if your orientation is `rows`. The Japanese writes the YAML value as `row` (singular) in code formatting.
findings.reader_consequence: A Japanese reader copying the code-formatted value writes `orientation: row`, which flexdashboard does not accept as the row layout, and the dashboard falls back to the default orientation with no obvious error.
